course: AWS Certified Generative AI Developer – Professional (AIP-C01)
part_title: Lab 11 — Troubleshoot Unsafe Input, Prompt Injection and Output Leakage
review_basis: Original checked-in source WebPs 62–67 inspected: trust boundaries, guardrail versions, scoped tools, streaming buffering, masked logs and safety regression cases.

scenes.title: Scenario and trust-boundary map
scenes.narration: The lab begins with a user trying to override application policy and obtain a dummy sensitive identifier. A retrieved document also contains an instruction-like string attempting to redirect the model. Follow the trust boundaries carefully. User input is untrusted; the application backend validates identity and permissions. The Knowledge Base may return useful reference data, but retrieved text is also untrusted data, not a new system instruction. The model is invoked with a specifically configured Bedrock Guardrail, and tool permissions remain scoped independently of the model's wishes. Before any response is displayed, the application applies output checks and an appropriate streaming safety buffer. The sample logs show a guardrail identifier and version and masked identifier content; those values are synthetic. Open the guardrail configuration and record the version used by the failing invocation, not merely the version displayed as latest. The goal is to prove that user instructions, document text, tool results and model output cross their trust boundaries with the correct checks. This requires both guardrail policies and application authorization, logging and display behavior.

scenes.title: Reproduce with synthetic redacted evidence
scenes.narration: Use only the sandbox's synthetic identifier fixture. First submit a benign request as a control, then a test prompt that attempts to ignore previous instructions and disclose the dummy customer ID. The image also shows injected text inside retrieved content, so test the case where the attack enters through a document rather than directly through the user. Open the Bedrock playground with the intended guardrail identifier and version, and review the resulting CloudWatch events. The sample includes guardrail_invoked, input_check identifying prompt injection, a model response with guardrail intervention, an unauthorized tool call denied, and a sanitized log where the dummy ID is masked. Distinguish a safe model refusal from a tool authorization denial: the tool must remain inaccessible even if the model attempts to call it. If the guardrail isn't present in the actual invocation, explicitly configure it in the application rather than assuming console test settings apply automatically. After a scoped repair, verify that the input is blocked or masked while the benign request still succeeds. Never put an actual customer identifier into reproduction logs.

scenes.title: Inspect guardrail version invocation and policy
scenes.narration: This slide separates guardrail enforcement from custom application processing. The application receives and routes a request, invokes Bedrock with an explicit guardrail identifier and guardrailVersion, and then performs its own buffering, formatting, citation checks and other post-processing. The pictured Converse example supplies a guardrailConfig referencing a specific version rather than relying on whichever version the console happens to display. Confirm the exact guardrail ID and version in the runtime request and in the redacted application log. Review supported policies: content filtering, denied topics, sensitive information and word filtering, and ensure the configured interventions match the exercise. The sample log records that a guardrail was applied and the response redacted. Crucially, output buffering is not a native toggle guaranteed by Bedrock Guardrails; it is an application-level control that you must implement. If unsafe tokens have already streamed to the user before application review, subsequent masking cannot undo the disclosure. Treat the guardrail as one layer in a defense-in-depth design rather than a replacement for IAM permissions or source authorization.

scenes.title: Enforce input retrieval tool and output controls
scenes.narration: Follow the six numbered stages across the top. First validate the user query, then retrieve only from approved documents under the user's identity. Third, treat retrieved text as untrusted context even when it came from your own S3 bucket. Fourth, constrain tool access to narrowly approved read or write actions independent of what the model requests. Fifth, apply the configured guardrail to relevant input and output, and sixth, verify citations and handle the response in your application before displaying it. The pseudocode illustrates allowed Knowledge Base search and explicit failed-citation handling; the adjacent rules require a citation, a buffering period, and a specified fallback when evidence is missing. Those are sample application policies, not native guardrail checkboxes. The response example shows a leave-policy answer with a citation and a two-second display buffer. Before copying such a design, decide whether the buffering time and citation criteria fit your interface. Validate with malicious, benign, unauthorized and no-evidence fixtures, and preserve the same authorization for any tool side effects.

scenes.title: Verify streaming and logging do not leak
scenes.narration: A blocked final response is not enough if sensitive content already appeared in streamed tokens or in raw logs. Trace the test prompt and an injected retrieved passage through the configured Bedrock Guardrail, the scoped tool output and the streaming application buffer. The slide's example tool result is denied with an out_of_scope reason, and the displayed response withholds the identifier while providing a safe explanation. In the streaming inspection pane, individual generated tokens are held and reviewed before release. Separately inspect CloudWatch application log events for user input, retrieved documents, guardrail action, tool result and output; confirm the identifier is masked rather than stored in cleartext. The negative case must be blocked without a stream or log leak, while a benign request should still pass. The sample guardrail console is illustrative: the buffering and log sanitation behavior belong to the application and need explicit regression tests. If a leak occurs, stop streaming before changing any policy thresholds; protect sensitive material first and then investigate the failing boundary.

scenes.title: Run safety and legitimate-task regression suite
scenes.narration: The final exercise checks both security and usability. Submit a synthetic instruction-injection attempt, a benign request to summarize an ordinary passage, and a dummy personally identifiable information fixture. The application architecture routes requests through safety checks, generation or streaming, and sanitized monitoring. The example safety configuration enables injection blocking, identifier masking, a limited set of allowed task types and application-level output buffering. It also avoids logging raw prompts while retaining redacted safety decisions. The regression output shows the attack blocked, the benign summarization allowed, and the identifier fields redacted. Do not define success as blocking everything; excessive false positives can make the system unusable. Add an authorized workflow test to verify that legitimate scoped tool operations remain permitted and that denied operations stay denied. Review false positives, false negatives, streaming release behavior and log masking together before promotion. Remove synthetic test data, temporary logs and caches when finished, preserving only the redacted evidence and regression results required for future audits.
